problem: Existing outdoor VLN datasets (Talk2Nav, Talk2Car, Touchdown) use only verbal instructions, while gesture-guided datasets (CAESAR, YouRefIt) target indoor referring-expression comprehension with short, simple instructions that need no multi-hop reasoning between gesture and language.
motivation: Humans naturally combine pointing gestures with speech, so interfaces for mobility robots (e.g., service robots) should support gesture-guided demonstrative instructions such as 'this cone' or 'that tall building'. Simulation allows scalable image and ground-truth capture, and MTurk allows free-form natural instructions instead of templates.
key_idea: Build GesNavi, a crowdsourced dataset of 3,100 free-form outdoor navigation instructions in a simulated Tokyo scene, where a gestured object (bounding box) serves as an intermediate anchor for multi-hop reasoning to a target object.
insight: The dataset shows humans tend to gesture at closer and larger objects (mean 11.5 m, ~25% larger boxes) as anchors to reach farther, smaller targets (12.2 m). Instructions average 13.1 words, versus 5.3 for CAESAR and 3.7 for YouRefIt, indicating more complex multi-hop language. No models are evaluated, so difficulty is only inferred from length and structure.
method: Image collection: automated virtual camera driving along roads in an AirSim/Unreal Engine replica of a dense 70,000 m2 Tokyo neighborhood, with placed vehicles, pedestrians, trees, cones and vending machines; varied lighting (morning, afternoon, evening); a human monitors to avoid duplicates and unnatural scenes.

Multi-perspective pairs: each capture has two images a few meters apart at a 45° relative angle; one is used for annotation and the other is a supplementary perspective mimicking a user standing outside the mobility.
Auto ground truth: depth maps, object classes, positions relative to the robot, and 2D/3D bounding boxes are extracted from the simulator.
Gesture simplification: pointing gestures are replaced by a bounding box on the gestured object, expected to come from gesture recognition in practice, which avoids costly VR-based capture.

MTurk annotation: annotators write free-form instructions to a target of their choice, draw a box on the gestured object as an intermediate anchor and a tight box on the target; 25 screened expert workers, batch reviews and feedback, $0.75 per image, about 10.7 min each.
Label assignment: gestured/target classes are assigned by highest IoU with ground-truth objects.

setting.observation: simulated RGB images (two perspectives per scene) with depth maps, plus gestured-object bounding box and text instruction
setting.action_space: not applicable (target object localization via bounding box; no agent actions defined)

numbers_note: Dataset paper with no model results; only dataset statistics (3,100 samples, 924-word vocabulary, mean length 13.1 words).
results: GesNavi contains 3,100 gesture-guided outdoor VLN instructions with a 924-word vocabulary and lengths of 6–34 words (mean 13.1), comparable to Talk2Car (11.0) and much longer than CAESAR-XL (5.3) and YouRefIt (3.7). Most frequent gestured object is Person (1350); most frequent target is Obstacle (334). No baselines are evaluated.
limitations: Uses simulated images only, limiting real-world realism and applicability
Gestures are simplified to a bounding box on a single object, ignoring raw hand motion and gestures referring to multiple objects or groups
No methods or baselines evaluated; difficulty is inferred only from instruction length
Dataset is small (3,100 samples) relative to CAESAR-XL
